title: PhD Studentships at the University of Leicester: Funded Population Health, Genetics and Healthcare Research Opportunities 2027
summary: The University of Leicester College of Life Sciences is offering PhD studentships for 2027 entry , providing an opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers to undertake advanced research in Population Health Sciences, Genetics, and Healthcare . The studentships cover four distinct research projects addressing important questions in diabetes and metabolic health, bacteriophage genome biology, nutrition and hearing health inequalities, and perinatal palliative care. Applicants are invited to review all four available projects and identify the research topic and supervisory team that best matches their academic background and research interests. The application deadline is 5 October 2026 , and the successful studentships are scheduled to begin on 4 January 2027 . The opportunity is particularly relevant to prospective PhD researchers interested in health sciences, public health, epidemiology, nutrition, genetics, molecular biology, healthcare research, health inequalities, and related interdisciplinary fields. What Are the University of Leicester College of Life Sciences PhD Studentships? The University of Leicester College of Life Sciences is offering doctoral studentships linked to four specific research projects. Rather than providing a single broad PhD topic, the opportunity allows applicants to choose from four defined projects. Each project has its own research question, supervisors, methodology and expected contribution to the relevant field. The four projects are: Exploring ethnic differences in adipose tissue composition and characteristics after weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes Dissection of the usage and function of unique genome architecture encoded by Burkholderia phage Matilda Diet, insulin resistance and hearing loss in England: investigating a socioeconomic pathway in older adults Perinatal palliative care in practice: an ethnographic study Projects 1 and 3 are within Population Health Sciences , Project 2 is within Genetics , and Project 4 is within Healthcare . Project 1: Ethnic Differences in Adipose Tissue After Weight Loss in Type 2 Diabetes Research area: Population Health Sciences Supervisors Dr Gráinne Whelehan Professor Louise Goff Project title Exploring ethnic differences in adipose tissue composition and characteristics after weight loss in people with type 2 diabetes This PhD project focuses on the relationship between ethnicity, adiposity, metabolic health and type 2 diabetes remission . Type 2 diabetes disproportionately affects people of Black African and Caribbean ethnicity in the UK , who can develop the condition at lower levels of overall adiposity than White European populations. Interestingly, the source notes that Black African populations can have a more favourable distribution of adiposity, including lower levels of visceral and hepatic fat. This creates an important scientific question because conventional models often associate ectopic fat accumulation with the development and remission of type 2 diabetes. The project therefore seeks to understand why responses to intensive weight-loss interventions may differ between ethnic populations. Why Is This Research Important? Intensive dietary weight-loss interventions, including total diet replacement, have demonstrated substantial success in inducing remission of type 2 diabetes, particularly among predominantly White European populations. However, emerging real-world evidence from the NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission Programme suggests that improvements in blood glucose control and remission rates may be lower among Black African and Caribbean populations. The reasons for these differences remain unclear. The proposed PhD will investigate whether differences in response are related to: The amount of weight lost Changes in adipose tissue distribution Differences in adipose tissue characteristics Changes in visceral fat Changes in hepatic fat Changes in pancreatic fat Adipocyte characteristics Tissue metabolites Adipokines Inflammatory cytokines Substrate utilisation Basal metabolic rate Cardiometabolic risk markers Research Design The project will use a two-group observational design comparing Black African and Caribbean and White European men and women with type 2 diabetes who undergo a 12-week intensive weight-loss intervention. The intervention will target approximately 10% body-weight reduction . The primary outcome will be the change in HbA1c , which will be compared between the ethnic groups following the intervention. Researchers will also investigate changes in: Total body weight Fat mass Fat-free mass Visceral fat Hepatic fat Pancreatic fat Other aspects of body composition Magnetic resonance imaging will be used to quantify specific ectopic fat depots. Subcutaneous adipose tissue biopsies will also be analysed to investigate biological mechanisms associated with differences in metabolic response. Potential Contribution of the Project The research aims to determine whether reductions in ectopic fat and adipose tissue remodelling contribute to improvements in glycaemic control equally across ethnic groups. The findings could contribute to understanding whether existing diabetes remission strategies adequately address the biological characteristics of populations disproportionately affected by type 2 diabetes. The project could also provide evidence relevant to: NHS diabetes remission services Precision medicine Diabetes prevention and management Metabolic health Health inequalities Ethnic differences in disease progression and treatment response The project description identifies this as an important gap because many existing remission strategies have been developed largely from evidence involving White European populations. Project 2: Burkholderia Phage Matilda Genome Architecture Research area: Genetics Supervisors Dr Jessica Lewis Dr Andrew Millard Project title Dissection of the usage and function of unique genome architecture encoded by Burkholderia phage Matilda The second PhD project moves into genetics, microbiology and molecular biology. It focuses on jumbo bacteriophages , a group of bacteriophages characterised by unusually large genomes that can provide greater independence from their bacterial hosts. The project centres on a recently isolated jumbo phage known as φMatilda , which targets the lung pathogen Burkholderia cenocepacia . What Makes the Genome Interesting? The project description highlights a distinctive genome architecture in φMatilda. The genome contains two large bidirectional elements at its termini. These elements predominantly encode hypothetical proteins. They are surrounded by large inverted repeats measuring approximately: 1.3 kilobases 18 kilobases Although bidirectional elements and inverted repeats have been observed in some phage genomes, the combination and scale of these features have not previously been described in any organism according to the project description. The unusual architecture raises questions about whether these regions have an important biological function. What Will the PhD Research Investigate? The project aims to determine: The function of the terminal genome elements Their importance during infection Whether the inverted repeats cause physical rearrangement of the phage chromosome Whether the genome conformation is maintained across different bacterial hosts Which host factors influence genome architecture How the phage genome behaves during early infection Whether structural genome rearrangements are necessary for successful infection Researchers will generate phage deletion mutants targeting the bidirectional and inverted repeat sequences. The effects of these mutations on: Genome stability Infection dynamics Genome conformation will then be assessed. Research Techniques The project proposes a combination of advanced research approaches, including: Transcriptomics Microscopy DNA conformation capture Hi-C Phage genetic manipulation Host mutant generation Infection experiments Genome architecture analysis The research could contribute to understanding the biology of jumbo phages and provide broader insights into DNA structure and genome organisation. Project 3: Diet, Insulin Resistance and Hearing Loss in Older Adults Research area: Population Health Sciences Supervisors Dr Dalia Tsimpida Professor Louise Goff Project title Diet, insulin resistance and hearing loss in England: investigating a socioeconomic pathway in older adults The third project combines nutritional epidemiology, metabolic health, hearing health and social epidemiology . It examines whether diet and metabolic health may help explain socioeconomic inequalities in hearing loss among older adults in England. Why Study Diet and Hearing Loss? Hearing loss affects more than nine million adults in England and is strongly patterned by socioeconomic circumstances. According to the project description, people in the most disadvantaged groups can be up to twice as likely to experience hearing decline in later life. However, the mechanisms behind this socioeconomic inequality are not fully understood. The project proposes that diet could represent an important and potentially modifiable pathway. The inner ear requires a continuous glucose supply. Poor glycaemic control can damage the small blood vessels supplying the cochlea, potentially affecting the auditory cells that depend on them. The project further identifies diets high in refined carbohydrates as a potential contributor to insulin resistance and chronic inflammation, which are associated with cochlear vascular injury. At the same time, dietary quality is socially patterned, with poorer diets more prevalent among lower socioeconomic groups. This creates a potential pathway linking socioeconomic circumstances, diet, metabolic health and hearing outcomes. Using the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing The project will use data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) . ELSA is a nationally representative cohort of adults aged 50 and over and includes information such as: Objective audiometric assessments HbA1c Dietary measures Other biomarker information Repeated measurements across multiple waves The research will proceed in three major stages. Stage 1: Developing a Dietary Metabolic Risk Index The student will construct and validate a dietary metabolic risk index. This index will then be examined in relation to: HbA1c BMI Stage 2: Examining Hearing Decline Mixed-effects modelling will be used to investigate whether the dietary metabolic risk index predicts hearing decline while accounting for important confounding factors. Stage 3: Causal Mediation Analysis The project will then use causal mediation analysis to determine whether the dietary-metabolic pathway accounts for part of the socioeconomic gradient in hearing loss. Additional analyses will be stratified by: Deprivation Sex Age Potential Impact The project is presented as the first study to integrate the social epidemiology of hearing loss with nutritional epidemiology using a UK longitudinal cohort. Its findings could contribute to evidence informing: NHS Health Checks Dietary guidance Hearing health policy Prevention strategies Health inequalities research Nutritional epidemiology Healthy ageing The project combines the supervisory expertise of Dr Dalia Tsimpida in hearing health inequalities and Professor Louise Goff in dietary composition and insulin sensitivity. Project 4: Perinatal Palliative Care in Practice Research area: Healthcare Supervisors Dr Katie Gallagher Dr Sarah Seaton Project title Perinatal palliative care in practice: an ethnographic study The fourth PhD project focuses on perinatal palliative care, neonatal mortality, parental support, healthcare decision-making and health inequalities . It proposes an ethnographic study examining how perinatal palliative care is delivered in practice. Why Is This Research Important? The project description reports that approximately 1,200 babies died during the neonatal period in 2023, equivalent to 2.9 deaths per 1,000 live births. The neonatal period refers to the first 28 days of life. The project also highlights differences in neonatal mortality according to ethnicity, with particularly high rates reported among babies of Pakistani, Black African and Bangladeshi ethnicity compared with babies of White ethnicity. Deprivation further compounds these inequalities. Causes of Neonatal Death The project identifies several major causes of neonatal death, including: Complications of prematurity Congenital anomalies Infections Complications arising during labour For families whose baby is diagnosed with a congenital anomaly, the diagnosis may occur during pregnancy. Prenatal diagnosis can have a significant emotional and psychological effect on families and may contribute to distress and depression among mothers. Parents may also need additional information to understand the diagnosis and navigate uncertainty even after receiving counselling about fetal anomalies. What Will the Perinatal Palliative Care PhD Investigate? The project proposes ethnographic research focused on what perinatal palliative care looks like in real-world practice. The research will examine: Information sharing Parental support Decision-making Care practices Access to care Differences in service provision Differences between families from different ethnic backgrounds Differences between families from different socioeconomic backgrounds Potential health inequalities in perinatal palliative care The research will be conducted in one NHS Trust in an ethnically diverse part of England , with the intention of ensuring representation of families from different backgrounds. Potential Impact of the Research The project aims to generate insight into perinatal palliative care practice and work with relevant stakeholders to develop guidance that could support national implementation. Potential areas of impact include: Parental mental health Care choices for babies following birth Healthcare decision-making Information provision Palliative care services Health equity National healthcare guidance Ultimately, the project seeks to contribute to future perinatal palliative care provision so that families can receive appropriate and equitable support during an extremely challenging period. Why These Four Projects Are Significant Although the projects are located in different disciplines, they share a broader focus on understanding important health and biological questions. The Genetics project investigates an unusual form of genome architecture in a bacteriophage and its potential role during infection. title: 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators: Up to €100,000 for Women Entrepreneurs Driving Innovation and Impact
summary: Women entrepreneurs and innovators developing solutions with the potential to transform industries, communities and society have an opportunity to gain major European recognition through the 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators . Jointly awarded by the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) and the European Innovation Council (EIC) , the prestigious prize celebrates women who are turning innovative ideas into successful businesses, practical solutions and measurable societal, economic and environmental impact. The 2027 edition features three award categories and offers financial prizes of up to €100,000 , alongside international visibility and opportunities to showcase an innovation journey to a European audience. Applications opened on 2 September 2026 and the deadline for submissions is 1 December 2026 at 17:00 CET . What Is the European Prize for Women Innovators? The European Prize for Women Innovators is an initiative designed to recognise and celebrate women whose entrepreneurial and innovative work is contributing to Europe s future. The award focuses on women who have moved beyond simply developing ideas and are using innovation to create tangible value. This can include innovations that generate economic opportunities, address societal challenges, improve people s lives, strengthen communities, protect the environment or introduce new technologies and business models. The initiative is jointly awarded by the European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) and the European Innovation Council (EIC) . Its broader purpose is to increase recognition of women in innovation and entrepreneurship while helping to address the gender gap that continues to exist across innovation ecosystems. According to the organisers, women innovators across Europe are developing solutions in areas ranging from deep technology and digital innovation to health, climate and other fields with significant societal and economic relevance. Why the 2027 Prize Matters for Women Innovators Recognition through a major European innovation prize can provide more than a financial award. For entrepreneurs building innovative businesses, external recognition can help communicate the significance of their work to potential partners, investors, customers, institutions and wider professional networks. The EIT describes the prize as an opportunity to gain European recognition for the impact of one s work and to inspire future generations of innovators. Applicants who receive recognition through the competition can potentially benefit from: Greater visibility for their innovation or business. Recognition at the European level. An opportunity to communicate their entrepreneurial journey. Increased exposure to innovation and entrepreneurship networks. Recognition of their societal, economic or environmental impact. A platform for highlighting women’s contributions to innovation. The opportunity to inspire other women and girls to pursue innovation and entrepreneurship. Significant financial prizes for successful applicants. The prize therefore combines financial recognition, visibility and the broader recognition of women s contributions to Europe s innovation ecosystem. Click here to apply 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators: Award Categories The 2027 competition is divided into three categories , each targeting a different group of women innovators and leaders. 1. EIC Women Innovators The Women Innovators category is intended for women founders and co-founders who have developed innovative businesses and are creating meaningful impact. This category carries the largest financial awards in the 2027 competition. Prizes First prize: €100,000 Second prize: €70,000 Third prize: €50,000 The category is particularly relevant to women who have progressed from developing an innovative concept to establishing or co-founding a business around that innovation. Applicants should therefore be able to demonstrate more than an interesting idea. Their work should show evidence of innovation, entrepreneurship and meaningful impact. 2. EIC Rising Innovators The Rising Innovators category focuses on younger women who are demonstrating significant promise as innovators. It provides an opportunity for emerging women innovators to gain recognition while still at an earlier stage of their innovation and entrepreneurial journey. A central eligibility requirement for this category is that applicants must be under 35 years old , subject to the complete conditions contained in the official contest rules. Prizes First prize: €50,000 Second prize: €30,000 Third prize: €20,000 This category is particularly relevant to younger women developing innovative technologies, businesses, research-based solutions or other forms of innovation capable of generating meaningful impact. 3. EIT Women Leadership The third category is the EIT Women Leadership category. This category is designed for exceptional women within the EIT Community whose innovation and leadership are making a strong impact. Unlike the broader Women Innovators and Rising Innovators categories, this award specifically relates to membership and participation within the EIT Community. Prizes First prize: €50,000 Second prize: €30,000 Third prize: €20,000 Women considering this category should carefully examine the official rules concerning EIT Community membership and the other eligibility requirements before submitting an application. Who Should Consider Applying? The prize is particularly relevant to women who are combining innovation, entrepreneurship and measurable impact . Potential applicants may include women who are: Founders of innovative companies. Co-founders of innovative companies. Entrepreneurs commercialising innovative technologies. Women developing digital innovations. Women working in deep-tech innovation. Women creating solutions in health and healthcare. Women developing climate or environmental innovations. Women building businesses around research and technology. Young women innovators under 35. Women within the EIT Community demonstrating exceptional innovation leadership. The innovation itself does not appear to be restricted to one particular industry. The EIT specifically identifies fields including deep tech, digital innovation, health and climate, while also describing the prize more broadly as recognising innovations delivering tangible results. This means that applicants should consider not only the sector in which they operate, but also the nature, originality and impact of their innovation. What Makes an Innovation Relevant to the Prize? The European Prize for Women Innovators is fundamentally concerned with innovation and impact. A strong application should therefore be able to communicate the connection between the applicant, her innovation, her business or entrepreneurial activity, and the results generated by that work. Important dimensions to consider include: Innovation What is genuinely new, improved or transformative about the solution? Applicants should be able to explain the innovative component of their work clearly rather than relying solely on technical terminology. Entrepreneurship How has the innovation been translated into a business, organisation, product, service or scalable solution? For founders and co-founders, the relationship between the innovation and the business should be clear. Impact What difference is the innovation making? Impact may relate to: Society. The economy. The environment. Communities. Customers or users. Industry. Public services. Quality of life. Sustainability. Leadership Applicants should also consider the role they personally played in turning an idea or innovation into a functioning solution. The prize is not simply about technological development. It celebrates the women behind innovations and successful businesses. Visit here for more information about the 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators Innovation With Societal, Economic and Environmental Value One of the important features of the prize is its emphasis on impact. The EIT describes the award as recognising women innovators whose work creates value for society, the economy and the planet . This broad framing means that innovation can have different forms of value. For example, an innovation could contribute to economic development through a new business model, create employment, improve productivity or open a new market. Another innovation might have social value by improving access to essential services or addressing a significant community challenge. An environmental innovation might contribute to climate action, resource efficiency, sustainability or environmental protection. The important consideration is the demonstrable relationship between the innovation and the impact it produces. Application Deadline for the 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators The application period for the 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators runs from: Opening date: 2 September 2026 Application deadline: 1 December 2026 at 17:00 CET Applicants should not wait until the final day to begin preparing their submissions. The eligibility rules, supporting information and application requirements should be reviewed carefully before submission. Important Dates Applicants should keep the following dates in mind: Date Event 2 September 2026 Applications open 17 September 2026, 11:00 CEST Information session 1 December 2026, 17:00 CET Application deadline Second quarter of 2027 Award ceremony An information session was scheduled for 17 September 2026 at 11:00 CEST , providing prospective applicants with an opportunity to learn more about the prize. How to Apply for the European Prize for Women Innovators Applications are submitted through the European Commission s Funding Tenders Opportunities Portal . Applicants should first determine which of the three categories corresponds to their circumstances: EIC Women Innovators EIC Rising Innovators EIT Women Leadership The relevant application portal should then be used to submit the application. The official competition rules should be reviewed carefully before submission because eligibility requirements can differ between categories. EIC Women Innovators application portal EIC Rising Innovators application portal EIT Women Leadership application portal Review the Official Contest Rules Before Applying The announcement directs prospective applicants to the official Rules of the Contest . This is particularly important because the webpage provides a high-level overview of the opportunity, while the formal rules establish the detailed legal and eligibility conditions governing participation. Applicants should therefore verify: Whether they satisfy the geographic eligibility requirements. Whether their organisation or company meets the applicable requirements. Whether they qualify as a founder or co-founder where required. Whether they satisfy the age requirement for the Rising Innovators category. Whether they meet any requirements relating to the EIT Community for the EIT Women Leadership category. Whether their innovation satisfies the competition s requirements. Whether all required information and supporting materials are provided. Whether the application is submitted before the stated deadline. Official Rules of the Contest (PDF) Areas of Innovation Highlighted by the Prize The 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators is not limited to a single technology or industry. The EIT highlights several areas in which women are creating significant innovations, including: Deep technology Deep-tech entrepreneurs developing advanced technological solutions can find particular relevance in this opportunity, especially where their technologies are being translated into practical applications and businesses. Digital innovation Women developing digital products, platforms, technologies and services can also fall within the broader innovation landscape recognised by the prize. Health Innovations addressing healthcare, health technologies and related challenges are among the areas specifically referenced by the EIT. Climate and environmental innovation Solutions addressing climate-related challenges and environmental sustainability also align with the areas highlighted by the organisers. Other innovative fields The prize s stated focus extends beyond these examples. The central consideration is the innovative nature and impact of the applicant s work. Why Recognition Matters Beyond the Prize Money Although the financial awards are substantial, the significance of the European Prize for Women Innovators extends beyond the monetary component. For an entrepreneur, recognition at European level can become part of the company s broader institutional and commercial profile. Recognition can potentially be useful when communicating with: Investors. Business partners. Research institutions. Customers. Public-sector organisations. Innovation networks. Other entrepreneurs. Media organisations. Potential collaborators. For emerging innovators, recognition can also provide a way of establishing a stronger professional profile within Europe s wider innovation ecosystem. The EIT specifically positions the prize as a mechanism for showcasing women who are transforming bold ideas into real-world solutions. Inspiring the Next Generation of Women Innovators Another important objective of the prize is representation. The initiative seeks not only to recognise current innovators but also to highlight women whose work can encourage future generations to participate in innovation and entrepreneurship. This is particularly significant in fields where women remain underrepresented. By highlighting successful women founders, entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators, the prize creates visibility around the different pathways through which women can contribute to technological, economic, environmental and social progress. Key Facts at a Glance Opportunity: 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators Organisers: European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) and European Innovation Council (EIC) Application opening: 2 September 2026 Deadline: 1 December 2026 at 17:00 CET Award ceremony: Second quarter of 2027 Number of categories: Three Categories: Women Innovators, Rising Innovators and EIT Women Leadership Highest individual prize: €100,000 Women Innovators prizes: €100,000, €70,000 and €50,000 Rising Innovators prizes: €50,000, €30,000 and €20,000 EIT Women Leadership prizes: €50,000, €30,000 and €20,000 Rising Innovators age requirement: Under 35, subject to the official rules Application platform: European Commission Funding Tenders Opportunities Portal Primary focus: Innovation, entrepreneurship, leadership and measurable impact Discover more global women s innovation programs here Final Thoughts The 2027 European Prize for Women Innovators provides a significant European platform for women who are converting innovative ideas into businesses, technologies and solutions with real-world impact. With three distinct categories, the competition accommodates established women founders, younger emerging innovators and exceptional women leaders within the EIT Community. The financial awards range from €20,000 to €100,000 , while the broader opportunity offers recognition and visibility within Europe s innovation ecosystem. Women considering applying should first identify the category that corresponds to their circumstances and then carefully examine the official Rules of the Contest. Particular attention should be given to geographic eligibility, age requirements where applicable, founder or co-founder requirements, EIT Community requirements and all application conditions. Most importantly, prospective applicants should ensure that their application clearly communicates what their innovation is, why it is innovative, what role they played in developing it, how it has been translated into practice, and what measurable value or impact it has created . With applications closing on 1 December 2026 at 17:00 CET , eligible women innovators who intend to participate should prepare and submit their applications before the deadline. title: School for Advanced Research Resident Scholars 2026–2027: Fellowships, Stipends, Eligibility, Application Process and Deadline
summary: The School for Advanced Research (SAR) offers residential fellowships for scholars whose research has reached a stage where they need dedicated time, space, and an intellectually collaborative environment to complete a major scholarly project. Based in Santa Fe, New Mexico, SAR supports research across the humanities, social sciences, archaeology, anthropology, history, sociology, and related fields, with particular emphasis on empirically grounded scholarship and work that contributes meaningfully to the understanding of humankind. The SAR Resident Scholars program is designed for researchers who have completed substantial portions of their research and now require an extended period to transform that research into a dissertation, book manuscript, or another substantial scholarly work. For the 2026–2027 academic cycle , SAR continues its long-running residential fellowship program, offering opportunities for doctoral candidates, postdoctoral scholars, senior scholars, Native American scholars, and scholars working in related humanities and social science disciplines. School for Advanced Research Resident Scholars Program For more than five decades, the School for Advanced Research has provided fellowships to scholars at advanced stages of research and writing. The program is particularly focused on giving researchers the time and intellectual environment necessary to bring substantial projects toward completion. Unlike opportunities that primarily fund the beginning of a research project, SAR s Resident Scholar fellowships are intended for scholars who have already undertaken significant research and need concentrated time to complete their dissertations, books, or other major scholarly works. The program combines: Financial support through a fellowship stipend Residential accommodation An interdisciplinary scholarly community Dedicated time for research and writing Opportunities for intellectual exchange Informal mentoring between senior and junior scholars Access to the broader intellectual environment of the School for Advanced Research SAR explains that proposed projects should generally require nine months to reach substantial completion . In certain circumstances, faculty applicants may be considered for semester-long, 4.5-month fellowships , depending on the availability of fellow apartments. Who Can Apply? The Resident Scholars program is intended for scholars working in the humanities, social sciences, archaeology, anthropology, and closely related fields. Eligibility differs according to the particular fellowship. Potential applicants include: PhD candidates who are preparing to write their dissertations Scholars who already hold doctorates and are preparing book manuscripts Faculty members seeking a semester-long writing residency Senior scholars Junior scholars Anthropologists with doctoral degrees Native American scholars working in the humanities or social sciences Native American writers with substantial published work Applicants should carefully identify which SAR fellowship corresponds to their academic status, discipline, research project, and eligibility. Major SAR Resident Fellowships SAR currently lists several fellowship opportunities, although some historically offered fellowships are no longer accepting applications. 1. Weatherhead Fellowship The Weatherhead Fellowship provides two residential fellowships for scholars. Eligible applicants include: Scholars who hold doctoral degrees and intend to write their books PhD candidates who intend to write their dissertations The fellowship is therefore relevant to both established scholars and doctoral researchers at an advanced stage of their projects. Applicants should demonstrate that their proposed project is sufficiently developed and that the residency will allow them to make substantial progress toward completion. 2. Paloheimo Fellowship The Paloheimo Fellowship provides one nine-month residential fellowship. This fellowship is specifically open to: PhD candidates Doctoral researchers who plan to write their dissertations The nine-month residency provides an extended period for concentrated dissertation writing within SAR s interdisciplinary scholarly environment. 3. Katrin H. Lamon Fellowship The Katrin H. Lamon Fellowship provides one residential fellowship. This opportunity has a specific eligibility focus. It is available to: Native American scholars at the predoctoral level Native American scholars at the postdoctoral level Native American scholars working in the humanities Native American scholars working in the social sciences Native American writers with a substantial body of published work Because this fellowship has specific eligibility requirements, prospective applicants should determine whether they meet the fellowship s criteria before preparing an application. Fellowships That Are No Longer Accepting Applications SAR also identifies several previous fellowship programs that have now ended. Mellon Foundation Fellowship The Mellon Foundation Fellowship previously supported two residential fellowships. According to SAR, the fellowship sunset in 2024 and is no longer accepting applications. Wenner-Gren Fellowship The Wenner-Gren Fellowship previously provided one residential fellowship for anthropologists. SAR states that this fellowship sunset in 2025 and is no longer accepting applications. Barbara and Dennis Tedlock Fellowship The Barbara and Dennis Tedlock Fellowship is different from the general application-based fellowships. It is awarded annually by invitation to a distinguished senior scholar. Consequently, it is not presented as an ordinary open application opportunity for prospective applicants. Fellowship Duration The standard SAR Resident Scholar fellowship is designed around a nine-month residential period . SAR states that proposed projects should generally require approximately nine months to bring to substantial completion. There is also a possibility of a shorter 4.5-month fellowship for faculty members. However, these semester-long fellowships are considered on a case-by-case basis , depending on the availability of fellowship apartments. This means that applicants should not automatically assume that a shorter residency will be available. Fellowship Stipends SAR provides different stipend amounts depending on whether the scholar is classified as a senior or junior scholar. Senior Scholars For senior scholars: $70,000 for a nine-month fellowship $35,000 for a 4.5-month fellowship Junior Scholars For junior scholars: $50,000 for a nine-month fellowship These stipends provide substantial financial support during the residential writing period and are intended to give scholars the opportunity to devote significant time to completing their projects. Residential Requirement An important feature of the SAR program is that the fellowships are residential. Fellows are expected to be physically present at SAR for at least 90% of their appointments . This requirement is important because the program is structured around sustained participation in the SAR scholarly community rather than simply providing remote financial support. Applicants should therefore ensure that their professional and personal circumstances allow them to spend the required period in residence. Housing and Office Arrangements SAR provides campus apartments for each fellow . However, applicants should be aware of an important logistical detail concerning workspace. Due to ongoing construction on the SAR campus: Campus apartments are provided to fellows. Separate offices are not currently available. Fellows should therefore expect to work from their residential accommodations or other available spaces rather than receiving an individual separate office. This is particularly important for researchers who require specialized office or laboratory facilities and should be considered when planning the residency. Senior and Junior Scholar Interaction SAR s residential model encourages interaction between scholars at different stages of their careers. Senior fellows are expected to provide informal mentoring to junior fellows . This creates an environment where doctoral researchers and less-established scholars can interact with experienced academics working across different disciplines and research traditions. The interdisciplinary nature of the community is an important component of the fellowship experience. Fields and Areas of Research SAR describes its Resident Scholars program as covering a broad range of the humanities and social sciences. Resident scholars approach research from fields including: Archaeology Anthropology History Sociology Humanities Social sciences Related interdisciplinary fields SAR has a stated preference for empirically grounded work . However, the fellowship is not restricted to a single academic discipline or methodological tradition. The broad disciplinary scope allows applicants to present projects from different intellectual perspectives. How Applications Are Evaluated SAR states that applications are evaluated according to two overall criteria . Criterion 1: Contribution to Scholarship Reviewers consider whether the proposed project will significantly advance the area of scholarship on which it is focused . Applicants should therefore clearly explain: What the project is about What scholarly problem it addresses Why the research matters What contribution it will make How the completed work will advance existing scholarship The proposal should make the significance of the project understandable from the perspective of the applicant s chosen field or intellectual approach. Criterion 2: Accessible Scholarly Writing SAR also evaluates whether the application and the applicant s previous published work demonstrate an ability to write in a publicly accessible manner for non-specialists . This is an important feature of the program. Applicants are not evaluated solely on specialized academic expertise. Their ability to communicate scholarly ideas beyond a narrow specialist audience is also relevant. Applicants should therefore pay close attention to the clarity and accessibility of their writing when preparing their materials. Interdisciplinary Review Process Because SAR supports scholarship across a particularly broad range of the humanities and social sciences, reviewers are instructed to consider applications from the perspective of the approaches and fields that applicants are seeking to advance. SAR states that reviewers will not privilege their own personal scholarly preferences, including preferences related to: Discipline Subfield Research method Theory Professional perspective Instead, reviewers aim to evaluate each proposal from the intellectual perspective adopted by the applicant. This approach is particularly relevant to interdisciplinary researchers whose projects may not fit neatly into a single academic category. Application Deadline The SAR Resident Scholars application cycle follows an annual schedule. Deadline: The first Monday of November Applications submitted by the first Monday of November are considered for a residency beginning on September 1 of the following year . Awards are announced annually in March . For example, an application submitted by the first Monday of November in one application cycle is considered for a residency beginning the following September. Applicants should verify the exact calendar date for the relevant application year when preparing their application, because the date of the first Monday in November changes from year to year. When Are Awards Announced? SAR states that fellowship awards are announced annually in March . Successful applicants can therefore expect the selection process to conclude several months before the September residency begins. This schedule gives selected fellows time to make arrangements for relocation, housing-related logistics, professional commitments, and preparation for their period of residence. What Kind of Project Is Suitable? The SAR fellowship is particularly suited to projects that are already substantially developed and now require dedicated time for completion. Examples of potentially suitable projects include: A dissertation nearing its writing stage A book manuscript based on completed research A major scholarly monograph An advanced humanities research project An anthropology project moving from research toward manuscript completion An archaeology project requiring concentrated writing and synthesis A history or sociology manuscript based on substantial completed research The program is not primarily designed as a short-term introductory research grant. Applicants should be able to demonstrate that the proposed period at SAR will make a meaningful difference in bringing the project toward substantial completion. Why the Writing Stage Matters One of the defining characteristics of the SAR Resident Scholars program is its emphasis on the transition from research to a finished scholarly product. Researchers often complete fieldwork, archival research, interviews, data collection, or other forms of investigation but then face the challenge of turning that material into a coherent dissertation or book. SAR s residential model is designed to provide an extended period in which scholars can focus on that final stage. The fellowship can therefore be particularly relevant to researchers who need: Dedicated writing time An interruption from normal teaching or professional responsibilities An interdisciplinary intellectual environment Feedback and discussion with other scholars Time to organize extensive research materials An opportunity to complete a dissertation or manuscript Eligibility by Fellowship The eligibility structure can be summarized as follows: Fellowship Number Available Main Eligibility Weatherhead Fellowship 2 Doctorate-holding scholars writing books and PhD candidates writing dissertations Paloheimo Fellowship 1 PhD candidates writing dissertations Katrin H. Lamon Fellowship 1 Native American predoctoral/postdoctoral humanities or social science scholars and Native American writers with substantial published work Barbara and Dennis Tedlock Fellowship 1 annually by invitation Distinguished senior scholar Mellon Foundation Fellowship No longer accepting applications Fellowship sunset in 2024 Wenner-Gren Fellowship No longer accepting applications Fellowship sunset in 2025 Geographic Eligibility The information provided by SAR does not identify a general restriction to applicants from a particular country or continent for the Weatherhead or Paloheimo fellowships. The program is international in scholarly scope, and eligibility is primarily described in terms of: Academic status Doctoral status Research field Stage of the project Fellowship-specific requirements The Katrin H. Lamon Fellowship has a specific eligibility requirement concerning Native American scholars and writers . Applicants from outside the United States should therefore examine the official application requirements carefully, particularly regarding residency, immigration, and any administrative requirements associated with spending the fellowship period in the United States. Qualifications Applicants Should Demonstrate Although eligibility varies by fellowship, a competitive application should be able to demonstrate several important characteristics. Advanced Research The proposed project should be sufficiently advanced that a nine-month residency can bring it toward substantial completion. Clear Scholarly Contribution Applicants should explain how their project advances knowledge in its particular field. Strong Writing Ability Because SAR specifically evaluates applicants ability to communicate with non-specialists, the application should be clear, accessible, and well structured. Appropriate Academic Stage Applicants must meet the academic requirements of the specific fellowship. For example, doctoral candidates may be eligible for certain fellowships, while other opportunities are designed for scholars who already hold doctorates. Ability to Participate in Residence Fellows are expected to spend at least 90% of their appointment in residence. Applicants should therefore be prepared to relocate to Santa Fe, New Mexico, for the fellowship period. Location of the Fellowship The School for Advanced Research is located at: 660 Garcia Street Santa Fe, NM 87505 United States Santa Fe serves as the residential setting for the fellowship program. The location provides fellows with the opportunity to work within SAR s scholarly community while spending an extended period focused on their research and writing. What Applicants Should Consider Before Applying Before submitting an application, prospective fellows should consider several practical and academic questions: 1. Is the project sufficiently advanced? SAR is looking for projects that can make substantial progress during the fellowship period. 2. Can the project realistically reach substantial completion? Applicants should have a realistic writing and research plan for the nine-month residency. 3. Does the project fit the humanities or social sciences? SAR s Resident Scholar program is centered on these broad academic areas and related disciplines. 4. Can you meet the residency requirement? Fellows must be in residence for at least 90% of their appointments. 5. Can you write for non-specialists? The ability to communicate scholarship clearly to a broader audience is explicitly part of SAR s evaluation criteria. 6. Which fellowship matches your status? Applicants should distinguish among Weatherhead, Paloheimo, Lamon, and other opportunities rather than assuming that every fellowship has identical eligibility requirements.
